name: Buccal fat removal
lead: Buccal fat removal, also called bichectomy, buccal lipectomy or buccal fat pad extraction, is a cosmetic operation that takes out part of the buccal fat pad (Bichat's fat pad), a deep encapsulated pad of fat in each cheek. The aim is to slim the lower midface so the cheekbones and jawline read more clearly and the cheeks look more hollowed or contoured. It is usually done through a small incision inside the mouth, often under local anesthesia.[1][3][9]

Looksmaxxing communities discuss it as a hardmaxxing option for people who stay round-faced even when lean, because proponents say this deep pad does not shrink much with weight loss the way superficial facial fat does.[1] Surgical reviews describe it as generally safe when the surgeon works carefully around the local anatomy, while noting that the evidence base is mainly case series and small single-arm studies, and that the fat pad does not regrow after removal.[2][3][9]

Its popularity rose sharply in the early 2020s after a celebrity disclosure in 2021 and heavy discussion on Twitter and TikTok, reported by The New York Times in 2022.[9] The American Society of Plastic Surgeons began recording it in 2022 and logged 4,543 procedures that year.[9] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies and 308 patients reported an overall postoperative complication prevalence of 25%, mostly swelling, trismus and pain, with high heterogeneity between studies; serious events such as facial nerve paralysis, infection and hematoma were rare in that analysis.[4]

sections.h: What it is and how it is used to change appearance
paras: The cheek's appearance depends on bone structure, skin, superficial fat and deeper volume. In people whose cheeks stay full despite low body fat, the buccal fat pad is the structure usually blamed, and removing part of it reduces fullness below the cheekbone, which can make the face look narrower and the cheekbones, masseter region and jawline more defined.[1][3] Reviews describe the intended result as a reduction of volume in the lower third of the face with sharper contours.[3]

Wikipedia notes that the operation is often done on its own, and sometimes together with a facelift, chin implant, neck lift, chin liposuction or fat grafting.[9] In looksmaxxing discussion it is typically grouped with other hardmaxxing procedures and compared with options such as leaning out, jaw and chin work, and cheek implants.

The buccal fat pad is an encapsulated mass of fat lying between the buccinator muscle and superficial muscles such as the masseter and zygomaticus, and is distinct from the more superficial malar fat pad. It is described as having several lobes and extensions, and its anterior part surrounds the parotid duct. Proposed functions include aiding movement of the chewing muscles and cushioning facial muscles.[8]

A review explains that although the pad has similar histology to fat elsewhere, its fibrous capsule means it is not metabolised in the way other fat depots are, which is why proponents say it stays full in lean people.[1] A 2026 anatomical study of 20 bichectomy patients examined whether pad volume correlates with sex, body mass index, skin colour and age, how accurate preoperative ultrasound is, and how these factors relate to satisfaction and facial rejuvenation.[16]

Reviews describe an intraoral approach using blunt dissection and suction-assisted extraction of the pad. The aim is to reduce volume in the lower third of the face and sharpen contours.[1][3] Wikipedia describes the surgeon making an incision inside the cheek near the upper second molar, separating the buccinator muscle fibres without cutting them, teasing the fat out with external pressure, cauterising its base and suturing with dissolvable stitches. The operation takes about 30 minutes under local anesthesia, swelling lasts days and is often not visible from outside, and final results can take up to about three months.[9]

An 'extended' variant that also removes the buccal extension and part of the temporal extension has been described for more extreme cheek contouring.[7] A plastic-surgery paper titled 'The Five Ds for Safe and Effective Buccal Fat Removal' presents a framework aimed at safe practice.[17] Registered studies have examined an intraoral technique (n=40, begun 2016) and a hydrodissection technique (n=54, begun 2016).[10][20]

Postoperative care has also been studied: the 643-procedure series found that a compressive bandage was associated with fewer major complications, and a small case series of six patients reported on low-power laser photobiomodulation after bichectomy.[2][21]

The 643-procedure series reported that female patients sought removal more for aesthetic reasons and male patients more often for functional purposes.[2] Plastic surgeons quoted by media and summarised by Wikipedia describe the cheeks naturally losing volume with age, which they say is why the operation is generally discussed for people with persistently full lower cheeks.[9]

Forum threads from users in their twenties ask whether a still-rounded face will slim with age and leaner body composition before committing, and others describe getting lean first and then having the operation.[15][22]

A single-arm trial of 21 patients measured pain, swelling, trismus, facial volume, satisfaction and oral-health-related quality of life up to three months after partial removal.[6] A study of Chilean patients examined their perception of oral-health-related quality of life after bichectomy.[18] The case series of 643 procedures by two surgeons reported a low incidence of major complications, which fell further with use of a compressive bandage.[2]

Authors of the extended-bichectomy paper state that long-term results of conventional approaches are generally accepted to have limitations and that the operation does not always deliver satisfactory results.[7] Wikipedia notes that the effect is permanent, that long-term research is limited, and that removal may produce a gaunt appearance as cheeks lose volume with age.[9]

The 2025 meta-analysis listed edema (38.4% of the complications), trismus (30.1%), pain (19.4%), asymmetry (11.7%), and rarer facial nerve paralysis (about 1%), infection, hematoma and emphysema; all occurred postoperatively.[4] A literature review of bichectomy complications states that the operation is linked to potentially serious complications because of the local anatomy, with some sequelae temporary and some permanent.[1]

Wikipedia describes the main structural risks as injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which can cause partial facial paralysis, numbness or loss of taste, and damage to the parotid duct, which can cause a salivary fistula or saliva collection; in some people the duct runs deep to the fat pad.[9] Parotid duct injury and sialocele are reported as uncommon but significant, and case reports and a small series, including five cases treated with sialendoscopy in Brazil, describe salivary duct injury after facial cosmetic procedures including buccal fat removal.[5][19]

Because the fat pad does not regrow, the change is permanent.[9] Wikipedia lists reinjection of fat into the buccal space, dermal fat grafts and injectable fillers as ways people try to restore volume or to mimic the result without surgery, and notes that long-term health effects have not been well researched.[9]
A recurring point in surgical commentary and forum discussion is that cheeks lose volume with age, so a face that looks sculpted at 25 may look more hollow at 55.[9][12]

The pad was first described by Lorenz Heister in 1732 as a gland and identified as fat by Xavier Bichat in 1802.[9] Interest in cosmetic removal rose in the early 2020s: Chrissy Teigen disclosed in 2021 that she had had it done, and in 2022 The New York Times reported rising popularity linked to discussion on Twitter and TikTok, quoting a plastic surgeon who called it one of the classic celebrity secret plastic surgeries.[9]

Wikipedia records that online speculation about other celebrities having had it became a trend of its own, while stating that those claims are unconfirmed.[9] The procedure acquired the nickname 'Handsome Squidward surgery' online, a reference to a chiselled-face scene from SpongeBob SquarePants.[9] The American Society of Plastic Surgeons did not collect statistics on it until 2022, when its members performed 4,543 procedures, the lowest count among the facial procedures it tracked.[9]

Because it is purely cosmetic, insurance rarely covers it. Wikipedia cites an average cost of about $4,097 on RealSelf in 2023, with some procedures priced as low as $1,000, one surgeon telling The New York Times in 2022 that he charged $40,000 while others typically charged $7,000 to $16,000, and a medical tourist reportedly paying $600 in Tijuana in 2020.[9]

Human data include a single-arm CONSORT-guided trial in 21 patients,[6] a 643-case retrospective series,[2] a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies,[4] a 20-patient anatomical and ultrasound study,[16] and registered studies of intraoral and hydrodissection techniques.[10][20] Case reports and small series describe postoperative laser therapy and salivary duct injuries.[19][21] No randomised trial comparing removal with no treatment or with alternatives was found.

Forum threads ask whether leaning out is sufficient, whether the operation suits a particular face, and how long swelling lasts, and there are threads recounting results, a 'confirmed botch' and a procedure that 'went wrong'.[11][12][13][14] Members also discuss whether removal is advisable for a young person who still has rounder cheeks.[15] One user wrote a thread crediting getting lean plus the operation with improving his mental health.[22]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the procedure is debated as a way to get hollow cheeks, with threads about candidacy, results and botched outcomes.[11][12][13][14][15][22]

claims.claim: Buccal fat removal gives leaner, more sculpted cheeks that dieting cannot.
claims.believers: Proponents say the buccal pad does not shrink with leanness, so some lean people keep full cheeks, and report results in threads asking whether the operation is warranted.[11][15]
claims.experts: Reviews describe the pad as encapsulated and describe the intended lower-face volume reduction, and a 21-patient trial measured facial volume reduction after partial removal.[1][6]

claims.claim: Removal can leave a person looking gaunt or worse than before.
claims.believers: Threads such as 'gone wrong' and 'confirmed botch' reflect members warning that results can look worse, especially with ageing.[12][13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes removal may leave a gaunt look as cheeks naturally lose volume with age, and surgeons describe an extended removal as sometimes limited or unsatisfactory in results.[7][9]

claims.claim: The operation is low-risk and minor.
claims.believers: Members post recovery photos and multi-month updates of the operation in threads on the topic.[14]
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis found 25% prevalence of postoperative complications, mostly mild; rarer events include facial nerve paralysis, and parotid duct injury is reported.[4][5]

claims.claim: Fat grafting can restore volume if removal goes too far.
claims.believers: Community write-ups state that the pad will not return to normal but fat transfer can partly compensate.[15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fat injections, dermal fat grafts and fillers as alternatives and states the fat does not regrow; no trials of grafting after bichectomy were found.[9]

claims.claim: A compressive bandage after surgery lowers the chance of major complications.
claims.believers: Surgeons in the Brazilian series advocate bandaging after bichectomy.[2]
claims.experts: A retrospective series of 643 procedures reported a statistically significant decrease in major complications with bandage use, though it was not a randomised comparison.[2]

claims.claim: Staying lean will eventually thin out round cheeks without surgery.
claims.believers: Users in their twenties ask whether continued fat loss or age will slim the face, and some say getting lean was the first step before surgery.[15][22]
claims.experts: Reviews state the encapsulated pad is not metabolised like other fat depots, and Wikipedia notes cheeks lose volume with age.[1][9]

claims.claim: Buccal fat removal is a celebrity secret behind chiselled faces.
claims.believers: Online speculation names celebrities as having had it, an idea behind the 'Handsome Squidward surgery' nickname.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a 2021 public disclosure and a plastic surgeon's description to The New York Times of it as a classic celebrity secret surgery, while stating the other names are unconfirmed.[9]

card.summary: Intraoral removal of the cheek's buccal fat pad for a slimmer, hollower look; permanent, with a 25% pooled postoperative complication rate and no randomised trials.
card.note: Irreversible; facial nerve and parotid duct injury are reported, and a gaunt look with ageing is discussed.

quick.overview:
Buccal fat removal takes out part of the deep fat pad in each cheek through a small cut inside the mouth, aiming for a slimmer lower face and more visible cheekbone contour. It became widely discussed on social media in the early 2020s and is a common hardmaxxing topic on looksmaxxing forums.

Published evidence is mostly case series, a small single-arm trial and systematic reviews. Surgeons describe it as generally safe with careful anatomy, while forum users share both satisfied and botched outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The encapsulated pad is extracted by blunt dissection and suction through an intraoral incision, permanently reducing cheek volume. Because the pad is not lost with general weight loss, proponents say removal changes contour where dieting does not.
quick.risks: A 2025 meta-analysis of 308 patients reported 25% prevalence of postoperative complications, mainly swelling, trismus, pain and asymmetry, with rare facial nerve paralysis, infection or hematoma. Parotid duct injury is reported. The effect is permanent and may look gaunt with ageing, according to encyclopedia summaries.
